title: True Native Apps vs. Progressive Web Apps: The Difference For Developers and Their Users
summary: When you're comparing app builders, "native" and "PWA" can look like minor technical details. They aren't. A progressive web app is a website built to behave like an app. It can offer a home screen icon and offline support, but it runs through a web browser. That limits its access to device features, makes performance inconsistent across browsers and operating systems, and keeps it out of the Apple App Store entirely. A native app runs directly on iOS or Android, so it gets full access to things like the camera, GPS, Bluetooth, push notifications, and offline storage, and it can be published to the app stores. Hybrid apps sit in between: they're built with web technology but packaged for app stores. Because they still reach device features through a browser layer, users can feel the lag. Thunkable compiles true native apps for iOS and Android, so you won't have to rebuild later when you need App Store distribution, reliable notifications, or hardware access. The takeaway is to decide which kind of app your idea needs before you start building.
body_markdown:
When people compare app builders, “native” and “progressive web app” (PWA) appear as if they are just minor footnotes; the kind of technical detail you can look up later once you’ve picked a tool.


This is most definitely not the case.


Whether a builder produces a native app or a PWA can affect three important things:


1. What your app can actually do
2. Where it can live for your users
3. How it is able to perform


And all of that is before a single feature is even built.


## What is a progressive web app?


Remember this, as it is an incredibly important distinction for the functionality of your app: A progressive web app, or PWA, is **a website built to behave like an app** . Offline support and a home screen icon are both totally possible with a PWA, and on the surface, it can feel close to the real thing.


‍


However, a PWA only runs through a web browser engine rather than compiling to native code, and that distinction carries significant differences and limitations.


‍


PWAs, for instance, can’t be listed in the Apple App Store, which is[the most revenue-generating app store in the world](https://www.businessofapps.com/data/app-data-report/) . Because PWAs run through the browser, access to certain device capabilities and performance can vary depending on the browser and operating system.


## What is a true native app?


A native app is built to run directly on a mobile operating system like iOS or Android. Because it’s built for the device itself rather than running through a web browser, it can interact more directly with the phone’s features and operating system. That distinction is what unlocks full access to a mobile device’s different systems, such as:


‍


- The camera
- GPS
- Bluetooth
- Push notifications
- Offline storage
- True operating system performance capabilities


‍


Native apps also go through the same App Store review process as any other app, since app stores recognize them as full apps rather than as websites. Thunkable is one example of a platform that compiles this kind of true native app for iOS and Android directly from a project.


‍


## Where hybrid apps fit in


There is a third option between native and PWA: Hybrid apps.


‍


A hybrid app combines elements of web and native apps. Much of the app is built using web technology, but it’s packaged as a mobile app so it can be installed on a device and distributed through app stores.


‍


Hybrid apps sit in the middle drawer of a developer’s potential toolbox: More capable than a PWA, but still carrying a nice chunk of performance tradeoffs that come from routing through a browser instead of running as fully native code.


‍


Most importantly, while hybrid apps can talk to device systems like the camera and the others listed above, it does so through that browser translation layer, which is where performance lag and loss will be felt by users the most. As you might expect, this could make or break user adoption and retention in pretty substantial ways.


## Where Thunkable stands on app builders


Thunkable compiles a true native binary for iOS and Android from your project, which means what you build is what actually makes it to your users.


‍


Several no-code app builders are PWA-only, so their apps can only live on a phone’s home screen as a bookmark with an icon, with no path into the Apple App Store or Google Play. If the plan for your app includes App Store distribution, real push notifications, or hardware access, that path should be available from the start. Thunkable gives developers the ability to create true native apps, which avoids rebuilds from PWAs later.


‍


## The real question to ask before you build


The difference between a native app and a PWA often does not show up right away. It tends to show up the first time someone expects a notification and does not get one, or the first time an app needs camera access and the browser layer gets in the way, or the first time someone tries to list an app on the App Store and finds out it is not possible with the tool they chose. Knowing which kind of app you are building, and why that matters for your specific idea, is worth figuring out before you start.


‍
